tools.name: exec

format.definition:
start: pragma_source | plain_source
pragma_source: PRAGMA_LINE NEWLINE SOURCE
plain_source: SOURCE

PRAGMA_LINE: /[ \t]*\/\/ @exec:[^\r\n]*/
NEWLINE: /\r?\n/
SOURCE: /[\s\S]+/

tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.

tools.name: request_user_input
tools.description: Request user input for one to three short questions and wait for the response. This tool is only available in Plan mode.

questions.description: Questions to show the user. Prefer 1 and do not exceed 3

header.description: Short header label shown in the UI (12 or fewer chars).

options.description: Provide 2-3 mutually exclusive choices. Put the recommended option first and suffix its label with "(Recommended)". Do not include an "Other" option in this list; the client will add a free-form "Other" option automatically.

description.description: One short sentence explaining impact/tradeoff if selected.

question.description: Single-sentence prompt shown to the user.

tools.name: request_user_input_async
tools.description: Ask the user one or more questions during ongoing work. Use this tool only to request missing information, preferences, constraints, clarification, or approval. The tool returns immediately without ending the turn or waiting for a reply; any reply arrives asynchronously as a new user message. Keep questions concise, self-contained, and easy to understand, using a level of detail appropriate to the user and task. The UI always allows a free-text answer, including when suggested options are provided. A preselected option is not submitted automatically.

questions.description: One or more self-contained questions to present together, in display order.

options.description: Suggested answers, in display order. Put the recommended answer first; the first option is preselected by default. The user can select one option or enter a free-text answer. Do not include an Other option or a free-text placeholder; the UI provides free-text input automatically. Omit options for a free-text-only question.

title.description: The complete question shown to the user, including any context needed to answer it.

tools.name: send_message_to_user_async
tools.description: Send a concise message that needs the user's attention during ongoing work. The tool returns immediately without ending the turn or waiting for a reply; any reply arrives asynchronously as a new user message. Use this tool to report a critical blocker or a finding that may change the task's direction, or to answer a user question or status request received while work is still in progress. Use this tool when a message needs the user's immediate attention; use commentary for routine progress and intermediate context. Use clear formatting, such as bolding questions, to make requests easy to notice and answer.

message.description: The concise question or update to send to the user.

tools.name: clock
tools.description: Tools for reading and waiting on time.

tools.name: sleep
tools.description: Pause execution for a specified duration. The sleep ends early when new input arrives for the active turn. Returns the elapsed wall-clock time.

duration_ms.description: How long to sleep in milliseconds. Must be between 1 and 43200000.

tools.name: collaboration
tools.description: Tools for spawning and managing sub-agents.

tools.name: followup_task
tools.description: Send a follow-up task to an existing non-root target agent and trigger a turn if it is idle. If the target is already running, deliver the task promptly at message boundaries while sampling, or after the pending tool call completes.

message.description: Message text to send to the target agent.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to send a follow-up task to (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: interrupt_agent
tools.description: Interrupt an agent's current turn, if any, and return its previous status. The agent remains available for messages and follow-up tasks.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to interrupt (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List live agents in the current root thread tree. Optionally filter by task-path prefix.

path_prefix.description: Task-path prefix filter without a trailing slash. Omit to list all live agents.

tools.name: send_message
tools.description: Send a message to an existing agent. The message will be delivered promptly. Does not trigger a new turn.

message.description: Message text to queue on the target agent.

target.description: Relative or canonical task name to message (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: spawn_agent
tools.description:
Available model overrides (optional; inherited parent model is preferred):
- `gpt-6.2-sol`: Fast, go-to model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.2-astra`: Our most capable model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.1-sol`: Previous generation model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.1-terra`: Efficient model that excels at visual understanding and computer use. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-astra`: Previous generation model for complex coding and professional work. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
        Spawns an agent to work on the specified task. If your current task is `/root/task1` and you spawn_agent with task_name "task_3" the agent will have canonical task name `/root/task1/task_3`.
You are then able to refer to this agent as `task_3` or `/root/task1/task_3` interchangeably. However an agent `/root/task2/task_3` would only be able to communicate with this agent via its canonical name `/root/task1/task_3`.
The spawned agent will have the same tools as you and the ability to spawn its own subagents.

It will be able to send you and other running agents messages, and its final answer will be provided to you when it finishes.
The new agent's canonical task name will be provided to it along with the message.

Note that passing `fork_turns="none"` will not pass any surrounding context to the spawned subagent, which may cause the agent to lack the context it needs to complete its task, whereas `fork_turns="all"` will provide the subagent with all surrounding context.

fork_turns.description: Parent history to inherit. Defaults to `all`; use `none` to start without parent history. Only `all` and `none` are supported.

message.description: Initial plain-text task for the new agent.

model.description: Model override for the new agent. Omit unless an explicit override is needed.

reasoning_effort.description: Reasoning effort override for the new agent. Omit to inherit the parent effort.

task_name.description: Task name for the new agent. Use lowercase letters, digits, and underscores.

tools.name: wait_agent
tools.description: Wait for a mailbox update from any live agent, including queued messages and final-status notifications. The wait also ends early when new user input is steered into the active turn. Does not return the content; returns either a summary of which agents have updates (if any), an interruption summary for steered input, or a timeout summary if no activity arrives before the deadline.

timeout_ms.description: Timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000, min 10000, max 3600000.

<permissions instructions>
Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `workspace-write`: The sandbox permits reading files, and editing files in `cwd` and `writable_roots`. Editing files in other directories requires approval. Network access is restricted.
# Escalation Requests

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

- Pipes: |
- Logical operators: &&, ||
- Command separators: ;
- Subshell boundaries: (...), $(...)

Each resulting segment is evaluated independently for sandbox restrictions and approval requirements.

Example:

git pull | tee output.txt

This is treated as two command segments:

["git", "pull"]

["tee", "output.txt"]

Commands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.

## How to request escalation

IMPORTANT: To request approval to execute a command that will require escalated privileges:

- Provide the `sandbox_permissions` parameter with the value `"require_escalated"`
- Include a short question asking the user if they want to allow the action in `justification` parameter. e.g. "Do you want to download and install dependencies for this project?"
- Optionally suggest a `prefix_rule` - this will be shown to the user with an option to persist the rule approval for future sessions.

If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with "require_escalated". ALWAYS proceed to use the `justification` parameter - do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.

## When to request escalation

While commands are running inside the sandbox, here are some scenarios that will require escalation outside the sandbox:

- You need to run a command that writes to a directory that requires it (e.g. running tests that write to /var)
- You need to run a GUI app (e.g., open/xdg-open/osascript) to open browsers or files.
- If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with `require_escalated`. ALWAYS proceed to use the `sandbox_permissions` and `justification` parameters. do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.
- You are about to take a potentially destructive action such as an `rm` or `git reset` that the user did not explicitly ask for.
- Be judicious with escalating, but if completing the user's request requires it, you should do so - don't try and circumvent approvals by using other tools.

## prefix_rule guidance

When choosing a `prefix_rule`, request one that will allow you to fulfill similar requests from the user in the future without re-requesting escalation. It should be categorical and reasonably scoped to similar capabilities. You should rarely pass the entire command into `prefix_rule`.

### Banned prefix_rules 
Avoid requesting overly broad prefixes that the user would be ill-advised to approve. For example, do not request ["python3"], ["python", "-"], or other similar prefixes that would allow arbitrary scripting.
NEVER provide a prefix_rule argument for destructive commands like rm.
NEVER provide a prefix_rule if your command uses a heredoc or herestring. 

### Examples
Good examples of prefixes:
- ["npm", "run", "dev"]
- ["gh", "pr", "check"]
- ["cargo", "test"]


## Approved command prefixes
The following prefix rules have already been approved: - ["git", "add"]
- ["uv", "lock"]
- ["uv", "sync"]
- ["git", "commit"]
- ["git", "diff", "--cached", "--check"]
 The writable roots are `/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests`, `/tmp`.

<multi_agent_role>You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent. Your final answer will be the response to the user
All agents in the team have access to the same set of tools.

All agents share the same workspace, filesystem, and tool state, meaning any changes will be immediately reflected in your local state.

With `fork_turns="all"` (the default), the child can see the parent’s conversation up to the fork. With `"none"`, it starts without that conversation. In either case, the child receives its own role and task.

You will receive messages in the commentary channel in the form:
```
Message Type: MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
They will be preceded by a header of the form `assistant:<sender> to=/root`
Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"`.</multi_agent_role>

description: Turns planning/spec.md into planning/plan.md before any code is written - ordered build steps, each naming the spec lines it meets and the test written first, with the test plan inside the plan. Use when asked to plan the build from the spec, or to write or fix the test plan.

# Plan from the spec

Write `planning/plan.md` from `planning/spec.md`. Write no application code and no tests in this
step: the plan is read and corrected by a person before anything is built.

## Read first

- `planning/spec.md`: the numbered requirements (R-01, R-02, ...) and how each is checked.
- `CHALLENGE.md`, `docs/requirements.md`, `materials/office-policy.md` and `snapshot.schema.json`:
  the sources the spec was written from.
- The request exports in `materials/requests/`: open the ones a test case uses, and read their
  `message` text.

## Write `planning/plan.md` with these four sections

1. **Choices.** The runtime, the interface (a CLI, a service or a web application), the test
   command, and how the model provider is called. One line each, with its reason.
2. **Steps, in build order.** A numbered list. Each step names the spec lines it meets
   (`R-03, R-07`), the test from the test plan that is written first and seen to fail, and what is
   true when the step is done. The first step builds the mock provider the tests use. Each test
   belongs to one step only, so every step has a test that fails until that step's code exists.
3. **Test plan.** A table, one row per case:

   | Case | Input | Mock response | Expected facts | Source of the expected facts | Spec lines |
   |---|---|---|---|---|---|

   - One row for each case in `docs/requirements.md` § Verification: a complete request, missing
     dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun and
     changed source content; then the paraphrased synthetic request, a refusal or interrupted
     response, and a failed retry after a prior success.
   - **Input** names the export file (or the new message you author) that shows the case. Find it by
     reading the messages.
   - **Mock response** says what the mock provider returns for that case: a reply saved under
     `tests/mock_responses/`, an error, or a cut-off reply. No test calls the real provider.
   - **Expected facts** are the field values, status, owner and next action the case must produce.
     Write them from the message text and the office policy, never from running the code.
   - **Source of the expected facts** quotes the words of the message and the policy rule they
     come from.
4. **Coverage.** Every spec line, each with the step that builds it and the test or check that
   shows it. A spec line with no step or no test is listed under "Not yet covered", with the reason.

## Before you finish

- Every spec line appears in § Coverage with a step and a test, or under "Not yet covered".
- Every expected fact has a quote from a message or the policy beside it.
- Every case of § Verification has its own row.
- No step and no test needs `API_KEY`.
- No test is named by two steps.

Where a spec line is unclear, say so in the plan and ask the person; do not guess a rule.

subcommands — read them from this command. You are already inside the repo:
entire auto-detects it from the git origin remote, so never ask the user for the
repo name. Pass --repo only to target a DIFFERENT repo.

# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests

## The task
Northstar Labs receives access requests as free-text messages. Build a small runnable application that uses a language model to turn those messages into structured records and a review queue for the IT team. The supplied company, people and requests are fictional.

Read docs/requirements.md for the operating context and required behavior, materials/office-policy.md for review rules, and snapshot.schema.json for the record format. The 20 JSON exports in materials/requests/ are your starting data. Choose an interface suited to the IT team: a CLI, service or web application. Operators should be able to start intake, inspect completed results while other requests are pending, and resume unfinished work through the documented interface.

## What to submit
This brief ships as CHALLENGE.md; the README.md below is yours to write.

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| README.md | Setup, supported runtime/provider, exact intake/test/accuracy-check commands, environment-variable names, and how to inspect the queue |
| Source code and dependency lockfile | Runnable application, extraction prompt, schema and model request configuration |
| deliverables/extractions.jsonl | One current record per message: document_id, source_sha256, extraction (schema-conforming object, or null on error), status, owner, next_action, error (null on success), and response_source (`mock`, or the provider and model ID that produced the record) |
| deliverables/queue.json | The review queue linked to extraction records by document_id |
| deliverables/accuracy.md | Source-derived expected fields for the 20 supplied messages and one paraphrase you author; the field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules, factual-error reporting and model/configuration; distinguish mocked examples from any optional live observations |
| deliverables/request-evidence.json | Credential-redacted example model request showing the model ID and configuration used, plus the implemented response handling |
| deliverables/verification.md | Verification commands and assertions, their intended comparisons, operating limits, and any observed results or repairs clearly identified as such |
| Coding-session capture | Session record paired with the submitted commit, collected through the facilitator's capture setup |

## Submission
Commit and push the application, outputs and session capture to your repository's default branch. Submit only the root repository link (`https://github.com/<your-account>/<repository>`) through the Classroom assignment. The facilitator supplies the assignment and capture instructions.

Submit the implemented provider integration and source-grounded validation procedure. Use mocked responses for reproducible development examples, and label each recorded observation with its configuration and whether it used a mock or provider response. The committed deliverables may come from mocked or provider responses; each record's response_source says which.
# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.

## Record and review behavior

Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. # Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.

# Northstar access-request intake

A Python CLI turns exported free-text messages into schema-validated extraction records and an ordered human-review queue. It prepares requests for people; a named manager is a contact, and successful intake never means approval.

## Setup and tests

Supported environment: Python 3.11+ on a local POSIX filesystem; this submission was exercised with Python 3.12 on Linux. Install `uv`, then run from the repository root:

```bash
uv sync --frozen
. .venv/bin/activate
env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

`pyproject.toml` declares jsonschema; `uv.lock` locks it and its dependencies. Setup may download locked packages. Tests and mock intake need no credentials or network. The tests forbid sockets and any read of API_KEY, including in guarded CLI subprocesses. A real-provider authentication unit check injects an inert credential function and inspects the environment-reader source; it never calls that reader. Target one planned test with `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -k test_r53_contract -v`; zero discovered tests is not a pass.

## Reproducible mock intake and inspection

These commands run after activation from the repository root. Use a fresh database path for a fresh demonstration; rerunning the same input/configuration reuses completed valid work.

<!-- smoke -->
```bash
python3 -m intake run --input materials/requests --db var/demo.sqlite --provider mock --responses tests/mock_responses --output deliverables
python3 -m intake queue --db var/demo.sqlite --include-pending
python3 -m intake resume --db var/demo.sqlite --provider mock --responses tests/mock_responses
python3 -m intake retry --db var/demo.sqlite --document IT-010.json --provider mock --responses tests/mock_responses
python3 -m intake history --db var/demo.sqlite --document IT-010.json
python3 -m intake export --db var/demo.sqlite --output deliverables
```

`run` accepts a directory or one exported JSON file. `queue` reads committed current outcomes even while another CLI process is preparing other documents; `--include-pending` also shows pending/running work without pretending it has a completed business status. `history` retains every attempt with its source bytes/hash, configuration, policy identity and outcome. Inputs absent from a later batch remain present. A corrected message or relevant producing-settings change creates a new attempt; `--refresh` explicitly forces one. Explicit retry bypasses reuse, and a failed retry becomes the current error while previous success remains identifiable in history.

Run recovery with `resume` after a crash or deployment interruption. It continues pending work and running work whose claim expired; the default claim lifetime is request timeout + 5 seconds. An active claim is left alone. Resume reconstructs settings per document, supports parallel progress and refreshes work if prompt/schema/policy versions changed. An older or expired worker token cannot replace a newer claim's result. Pending work with changed settings is marked superseded in history rather than mislabelled as produced under those earlier settings.

Each error includes an actionable diagnostic and a reproducible `retry_command`; use that command against the same recorded database/configuration. CLI exit status is 0 on successful execution, 1 when current error records or failed accuracy comparisons remain, and 2 for command/input/configuration errors. A `needs-information` request is successful intake awaiting clarification, not an extraction error.

## Keyboard and screen-reader operation

Add `--format text` after any subcommand for labelled output in reading order. This mode uses ordinary terminal text with no color, animation, cursor control or timed input. Each queue entry starts with its document name and work state, followed by its routing, errors and retry guidance when available. In history, each attempt has its own state, source and producing settings. Use the terminal's screen-reader navigation commands to review earlier lines. Font size, contrast and cursor preferences are set in the terminal.

```bash
python3 -m intake --help
python3 -m intake queue --help
python3 -m intake queue --db var/demo.sqlite --include-pending --format text
python3 -m intake history --db var/demo.sqlite --document IT-010.json --format text
```

Use the same `--format text` option with `run`, `resume`, `retry`, `export` and `accuracy`. While intake or resume is active, inspect progress from a second terminal with `queue --include-pending`. Read the `Retry command` line under the failed document and run it to retry that document. `export --format text` identifies the published generation, and `accuracy --format text` gives the match count and report path. JSON remains the default for command output and the format of the machine-readable exports.

Use a keyboard-operable terminal exposing its text through the platform's accessibility services, such as Xfce Terminal with Orca on Linux. See the [Section 508 verification results](deliverables/verification.md#section-508-accessibility) for tested versions, workflows and pending checks.

## Provider configuration

Mock mode reads only saved JSON replies and the development manifest under `tests/mock_responses/`; it never reads API_KEY. `--script` selects another saved manifest. Reply sequences reset when a new mock process is created; the durable record of attempts remains in SQLite. The production extractor does not look up known filenames or import tests/expected. `--mock-gates` is a development-only directory of file barriers for repeatable process/interruption tests.

Implemented live configuration: OpenAI Responses API, explicit `--model` (the documented reference configuration is `gpt-4.1-mini`), HTTPS endpoint `https://api.openai.com/v1/responses`, structured JSON schema with strict mode, `store=false`, and `--max-output-tokens 4096`. The prompt is `intake/prompt.txt`, and the schema is `snapshot.schema.json`. The adapter validates completed responses, refusal content, malformed JSON, schema types and literal evidence before routing. It does not execute embedded source instructions.

For an optional live run, have the operator supply API_KEY through the environment and select `--provider openai --model gpt-4.1-mini`. This implementation session did not read a real key, call a real model, or observe live performance. `API_KEY` is the only application credential environment variable. Model/provider/endpoint/timeouts are CLI configuration, not inferred from environment variables; changing `--endpoint` requires a compatible HTTPS service. Authentication is loaded lazily only by the real adapter. Logs/errors/evidence omit credential values and untrusted provider error bodies.

`run`, `resume` and `retry` accept `--workers` (default 4), `--timeout` seconds (default 30), `--max-retries` (default 0) and `--retry-delay` seconds (default 1, exponential between retryable attempts). Retries are bounded per document. Request limits, temporary provider errors and timeouts affect the document involved while other workers can continue. There is no organization-wide quota coordinator. Request settings, prompt/schema hashes and policy hash are persisted; changes to relevant production/routing settings refresh affected results. Policy changes currently re-extract rather than optimize to rerouting alone.

Provider request and response fields were checked against the official [Responses reference](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/responses/methods/create), [structured outputs guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs) and [model documentation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-4.1-mini). `deliverables/request-evidence.json` is an intercepted real-adapter request backed by a saved mock reply, with credential redaction; it is not a live observation.

## Accuracy and source evidence

```bash
python3 -m intake accuracy --input materials/requests --synthetic tests/fixtures/IT-P01.json --expected tests/expected --responses tests/mock_responses --provider mock --output deliverables/accuracy.md
```

Expected facts were authored from the plan/messages/policy before extraction runs, separately from the mocked provider replies. The synthetic input uses filename IT-P01.json to match its stated identifier and preserve the plan's complete staging/read case. The report contains 20 supplied cases plus that paraphrase, exact source quotes, producing configuration and 11 non-purpose scalar comparisons per case (231 total). Missing/error or duplicate-case extraction counts as 11 mismatches; nulls count and comparisons are exact, case-sensitive, without normalization. Extra cases, routing errors and schema/evidence/issues problems are reported separately. Purpose prose is reviewed against source evidence separately; a faithful paraphrase is not rejected for differing wording. Nonliteral purpose output is flagged for manual semantic review rather than automatically declared factually wrong. The JSON findings are saved beside the Markdown report.

The mock result tests the pipeline, not live model accuracy. It cannot establish fresh-wording extraction quality or universal resistance to instruction attacks. Factual-error mutation tests deliberately change otherwise valid saved-response facts so copied or self-derived expectations cannot silently pass. No minimum accuracy score or latency/throughput threshold has been invented.

## Shared operation, history and publication limits

Support is for multiple CLI processes on one host sharing one local SQLite database and local output directory; multi-host and network-share locking are not supported. Transactions keep claims/current pointers coherent. Immutable attempts are separate from current outputs. The latest accepted ingestion order controls the current source revision; export timestamps are display metadata. A late response can be retained in earlier history but cannot replace a newer current document revision.

Exports are generated from one committed snapshot. An advisory publisher lock serializes snapshot-to-publication work. `deliverables/current` atomically selects an immutable `.generations/` directory, and `extractions.jsonl`/`queue.json` are stable links through it. A reader inspecting both files during concurrent publication must resolve and pin `current` once, then read both files in that directory. Abandoned unpublished generations may remain on disk after interruption; retain them for investigation. Export again to publish the latest database state. The database is authoritative between exports.

The source's ordinary 200–400 messages/day and roughly 2,000-message bursts are operating context, not measured capacity. Verification covers the 20 supplied messages, a paraphrase, controlled concurrency/failure/interruption scenarios, and a 200-word input. It includes no 2,000-message load test, distributed deployment check, power-loss durability certification, live quota test or live-model accuracy measurement. Generic free-text facts and attack intent still need human scrutiny; exact quotes and schema checks cannot prove all semantics.

See `deliverables/verification.md` for per-step red/green evidence, assertions and remaining external checks. Final facilitator session-capture pairing and Classroom submission are external acceptance work; the application and the mock suite do not perform them.

tests/expected/IT-004.json tests/expected/IT-019.json tests/expected/IT-016.json # Northstar access-request intake A Python CLI turns exported free-text messages into schema-validated extraction records and an ordered human-review queue. It prepares requests for people; a named manager is a contact, and successful intake never means approval. ## Setup and tests Supported environment: Python 3.11+ on a local POSIX filesystem; this submission was exercised with Python 3.12 on Linux. Install `uv`, then run from the repository root: ```bash uv sync --frozen . .venv/bin/activate env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v ``` `pyproject.toml` declares jsonschema; `uv.lock` locks it and its dependencies. Setup may download locked packages. Tests and mock intake need no credentials or network. The tests forbid sockets and any read of API_KEY, including in guarded CLI subprocesses. A real-provider authentication unit check injects an inert credential function and inspects the environment-reader source; it never calls that reader. Target one planned test with `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -k test_r53_contract -v`; zero discovered tests is not a pass. ## Reproducible mock intake and inspection These commands run after activation from the repository root. Use a fresh database path for a fresh demonstration; rerunning the same input/configuration reuses completed valid work. ```bash python3 -m intake run --input materials/requests --db var/demo.sqlite --provider mock --responses tests/mock_responses --output deliverables python3 -m intake queue --db var/demo.sqlite --include-pending python3 -m intake resume --db var/demo.sqlite --provider mock --responses tests/mock_responses python3 -m intake retry --db var/demo.sqlite --document IT-010.json --provider mock --responses tests/mock_responses python3 -m intake history --db var/demo.sqlite --document IT-010.json python3 -m intake export --db var/demo.sqlite --output deliverables ``` `run` accepts a directory or one exported JSON file. `queue` reads committed current outcomes even while another CLI process is preparing other documents; `--include-pending` also shows pending/running work without pretending it has a completed business status. `history` retains every attempt with its source bytes/hash, configuration, policy identity and outcome. Inputs absent from a later batch remain present. A corrected message or relevant producing-settings change creates a new attempt; `--refresh` explicitly forces one. Explicit retry bypasses reuse, and a failed retry becomes the current error while previous success remains identifiable in history. Run recovery with `resume` after a crash or deployment interruption. It continues pending work and running work whose claim expired; the default claim lifetime is request timeout + 5 seconds. An active claim is left alone. Resume reconstructs settings per document, supports parallel progress and refreshes work if prompt/schema/policy versions changed. An older or expired worker token cannot replace a newer claim's result. Pending work with changed settings is marked superseded in history rather than mislabelled as produced under those earlier settings. Each error includes an actionable diagnostic and a reproducible `retry_command`; use that command against the same recorded database/configuration. CLI exit status is 0 on successful execution, 1 when current error records or failed accuracy comparisons remain, and 2 for command/input/configuration errors. A `needs-information` request is successful intake awaiting clarification, not an extraction error. ## Keyboard and screen-reader operation Add `--format text` after any subcommand for labelled output in reading order. This mode uses ordinary terminal text with no color, animation, cursor control or timed input. Each queue entry starts with its document name and work state, followed by its routing, errors and retry guidance when available. In history, each attempt has its own state, source and producing settings. Use the terminal's screen-reader navigation commands to review earlier lines. Font size, contrast and cursor preferences are set in the terminal. ```bash python3 -m intake --help python3 -m intake queue --help python3 -m intake queue --db var/demo.sqlite --include-pending --format text python3 -m intake history --db var/demo.sqlite --document IT-010.json --format text ``` Use the same `--format text` option with `run`, `resume`, `retry`, `export` and `accuracy`. While intake or resume is active, inspect progress from a second terminal with `queue --include-pending`. Read the `Retry command` line under the failed document and run it to retry that document. `export --format text` identifies the published generation, and `accuracy --format text` gives the match count and report path. JSON remains the default for command output and the format of the machine-readable exports. Use a keyboard-operable terminal exposing its text through the platform's accessibility services, such as Xfce Terminal with Orca on Linux. See the [Section 508 verification results](deliverables/verification.md#section-508-accessibility) for tested versions, workflows and pending checks. ## Provider configuration Mock mode reads only saved JSON replies and the development manifest under `tests/mock_responses/`; it never reads API_KEY. `--script` selects another saved manifest. Reply sequences reset when a new mock process is created; the durable record of attempts remains in SQLite. The production extractor does not look up known filenames or import tests/expected. `--mock-gates` is a development-only directory of file barriers for repeatable process/interruption tests. Implemented live configuration: OpenAI Responses API, explicit `--model` (the documented reference configuration is `gpt-4.1-mini`), HTTPS endpoint `https://api.openai.com/v1/responses`, structured JSON schema with strict mode, `store=false`, and `--max-output-tokens 4096`. The prompt is `intake/prompt.txt`, and the schema is `snapshot.schema.json`. The adapter validates completed responses, refusal content, malformed JSON, schema types and literal evidence before routing. It does not execute embedded source instructions. For an optional live run, have the operator supply API_KEY through the environment and select `--provider openai --model gpt-4.1-mini`. This implementation session did not read a real key, call a real model, or observe live performance. `API_KEY` is the only application credential environment variable. Model/provider/endpoint/timeouts are CLI configuration, not inferred from environment variables; changing `--endpoint` requires a compatible HTTPS service. Authentication is loaded lazily only by the real adapter. Logs/errors/evidence omit credential values and untrusted provider error bodies. `run`, `resume` and `retry` accept `--workers` (default 4), `--timeout` seconds (default 30), `--max-retries` (default 0) and `--retry-delay` seconds (default 1, exponential between retryable attempts). Retries are bounded per document. Request limits, temporary provider errors and timeouts affect the document involved while other workers can continue. There is no organization-wide quota coordinator. Request settings, prompt/schema hashes and policy hash are persisted; changes to relevant production/routing settings refresh affected results. Policy changes currently re-extract rather than optimize to rerouting alone. Provider request and response fields were checked against the official [Responses reference](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/responses/methods/create), [structured outputs guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs) and [model documentation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-4.1-mini). `deliverables/request-evidence.json` is an intercepted real-adapter request backed by a saved mock reply, with credential redaction; it is not a live observation. ## Accuracy and source evidence ```bash python3 -m intake accuracy --input materials/requests --synthetic tests/fixtures/IT-P01.json --expected tests/expected --responses tests/mock_responses --provider mock --output deliverables/accuracy.md ``` Expected facts were authored from the plan/messages/policy before extraction runs, separately from the mocked provider replies. The synthetic input uses filename IT-P01.json to match its stated identifier and preserve the plan's complete staging/read case. The report contains 20 supplied cases plus that paraphrase, exact source quotes, producing configuration and 11 non-purpose scalar comparisons per case (231 total). Missing/error or duplicate-case extraction counts as 11 mismatches; nulls count and comparisons are exact, case-sensitive, without normalization. Extra cases, routing errors and schema/evidence/issues problems are reported separately. Purpose prose is reviewed against source evidence separately; a faithful paraphrase is not rejected for differing wording. Nonliteral purpose output is flagged for manual semantic review rather than automatically declared factually wrong. The JSON findings are saved beside the Markdown report. The mock result tests the pipeline, not live model accuracy. It cannot establish fresh-wording extraction quality or universal resistance to instruction attacks. Factual-error mutation tests deliberately change otherwise valid saved-response facts so copied or self-derived expectations cannot silently pass. No minimum accuracy score or latency/throughput threshold has been invented. ## Shared operation, history and publication limits Support is for multiple CLI processes on one host sharing one local SQLite database and local output directory; multi-host and network-share locking are not supported. Transactions keep claims/current pointers coherent. Immutable attempts are separate from current outputs. The latest accepted ingestion order controls the current source revision; export timestamps are display metadata. A late response can be retained in earlier history but cannot replace a newer current document revision. Exports are generated from one committed snapshot. An advisory publisher lock serializes snapshot-to-publication work. `deliverables/current` atomically selects an immutable `.generations/` directory, and `extractions.jsonl`/`queue.json` are stable links through it. A reader inspecting both files during concurrent publication must resolve and pin `current` once, then read both files in that directory. Abandoned unpublished generations may remain on disk after interruption; retain them for investigation. Export again to publish the latest database state. The database is authoritative between exports. The source's ordinary 200–400 messages/day and roughly 2,000-message bursts are operating context, not measured capacity. Verification covers the 20 supplied messages, a paraphrase, controlled concurrency/failure/interruption scenarios, and a 200-word input. It includes no 2,000-message load test, distributed deployment check, power-loss durability certification, live quota test or live-model accuracy measurement. Generic free-text facts and attack intent still need human scrutiny; exact quotes and schema checks cannot prove all semantics. See `deliverables/verification.md` for per-step red/green evidence, assertions and remaining external checks. Final facilitator session-capture pairing and Classroom submission are external acceptance work; the application and the mock suite do not perform them.

# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests

## The task
Northstar Labs receives access requests as free-text messages. Build a small runnable application that uses a language model to turn those messages into structured records and a review queue for the IT team. The supplied company, people and requests are fictional.

Read docs/requirements.md for the operating context and required behavior, materials/office-policy.md for review rules, and snapshot.schema.json for the record format. The 20 JSON exports in materials/requests/ are your starting data. Choose an interface suited to the IT team: a CLI, service or web application. Operators should be able to start intake, inspect completed results while other requests are pending, and resume unfinished work through the documented interface.

## What to submit
This brief ships as CHALLENGE.md; the README.md below is yours to write.

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| README.md | Setup, supported runtime/provider, exact intake/test/accuracy-check commands, environment-variable names, and how to inspect the queue |
| Source code and dependency lockfile | Runnable application, extraction prompt, schema and model request configuration |
| deliverables/extractions.jsonl | One current record per message: document_id, source_sha256, extraction (schema-conforming object, or null on error), status, owner, next_action, error (null on success), and response_source (`mock`, or the provider and model ID that produced the record) |
| deliverables/queue.json | The review queue linked to extraction records by document_id |
| deliverables/accuracy.md | Source-derived expected fields for the 20 supplied messages and one paraphrase you author; the field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules, factual-error reporting and model/configuration; distinguish mocked examples from any optional live observations |
| deliverables/request-evidence.json | Credential-redacted example model request showing the model ID and configuration used, plus the implemented response handling |
| deliverables/verification.md | Verification commands and assertions, their intended comparisons, operating limits, and any observed results or repairs clearly identified as such |
| Coding-session capture | Session record paired with the submitted commit, collected through the facilitator's capture setup |

## Submission
Commit and push the application, outputs and session capture to your repository's default branch. Submit only the root repository link (`https://github.com/<your-account>/<repository>`) through the Classroom assignment. The facilitator supplies the assignment and capture instructions.

Submit the implemented provider integration and source-grounded validation procedure. Use mocked responses for reproducible development examples, and label each recorded observation with its configuration and whether it used a mock or provider response. The committed deliverables may come from mocked or provider responses; each record's response_source says which.
# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.

## Record and review behavior
- Use a language model to extract the request details into records that conform to snapshot.schema.json.
- Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data. Preserve exact supporting quotes and represent uncertain fields as null with an explanatory issue.
- Use message content as the source of business facts. Preserve missing values, conflicting alternatives and explicit corrections according to the policy. Keep document identity distinct from the request ID stated in the message.
- Apply the supplied review policy and display each request's status, owner and next action. Approval decisions belong to the named human reviewers.
- Record input filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Reuse results when the source and relevant processing settings are unchanged, refresh affected results when those inputs or settings change, and retain earlier versions. Process each message independently and make failures visible with a reproducible retry command.
- Handle malformed output, provider errors, refusal and interrupted responses explicitly. Keep model/provider settings configurable and document a supported configuration. The facilitator supplies an API key through the environment variable API_KEY.

## Verification

Include automated tests covering a complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun, and changed source content. Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. Include checks for refusal or interrupted responses and a failed retry after a prior success.


Describe how your implementation supports the operating context above, and include checks for the operational situations your design handles. Record assumptions about workload and shared operation, the expected behavior during interruptions, and the limits of the verification you performed.
# Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.
# Block 1. Research: the brief as a spec

The brief is written as prose, across four files. Before you plan or write code, turn it into a
**spec**: a list of numbered requirements, each one sentence a test or an inspection can check,
each with the words of the brief it comes from and how you will check it. Block 2 plans from the
spec, and block 3 checks what Codex built against it, line by line. A requirement missing from the
spec is one nobody will build or check.

Start only after `python3 tools/check_prerequisites.py` prints `READY`
(`docs/00-prerequisites.md`).

## What to read

| File | What it gives the spec |
|---|---|
| `CHALLENGE.md` | the task, and the files you submit, each with what it must contain |
| `docs/requirements.md` | the operating context, record and review behaviour, and § Verification: the cases your tests must cover |
| `materials/office-policy.md` | the fields to extract, the five review-queue rules in order, processing and recovery |
| `snapshot.schema.json` | the record each extraction must match |
| `materials/requests/` | the 20 message exports; read three or four to see what the rules meet |

## Steps

1. Start Codex in the root of your clone: `codex`.
2. Ask Codex to read the four files and draft `planning/spec.md`. Your request says:
   - one numbered requirement per line, `R-01`, `R-02`, ..., each one testable sentence;
   - for each, the file and section it comes from, with the exact words quoted;
   - for each, how it will be checked: which test, which file to inspect, or which command to run;
   - nothing invented: a requirement the files do not state is not in the spec.

   <details><summary>An example request, if you want a starting point</summary>

   ```text
   Read CHALLENGE.md, docs/requirements.md, materials/office-policy.md and snapshot.schema.json.
   Write planning/spec.md: a table with columns ID, Requirement, Source, Check. One row per
   requirement, IDs R-01 onward. Requirement is one sentence that a test or an inspection can
   check. Source names the file and section and quotes the exact words. Check says how we will
   know it is met: the test, the file to inspect, or the command. Do not add anything the files
   do not say. Do not write any code.
   ```

   </details>

3. Read the draft against the files yourself. Codex misses requirements and merges two into one
   line. Check that these each have their own lines:
   - every fact the policy says to extract, and the rules for missing, conflicting and corrected values;
   - each of the five review-queue rules, in the policy's order;
   - each processing and recovery rule: errors, retries, hashes, reruns, changed input, history;
   - each file `CHALLENGE.md` asks you to submit;
   - each case `docs/requirements.md` § Verification lists.
4. **Research what the text leaves unclear.** Ask Codex to list every place where two readings are
   possible, or where a term is not defined. For each, look it up (in the files first, then in the
   documentation of the tool or standard it names) and write what you found. Add a section
   `## Open questions` to the spec: each question, what you found, and what stays open. Do not turn
   an open question into a requirement by guessing.
5. Commit the spec:

   ```bash
   git add planning/spec.md
   git commit -m "Spec: the brief as numbered requirements"
   ```

## What is on disk at the end

`planning/spec.md`, committed: the requirements table, then `## Open questions`.

## How to tell it is right

- Every row quotes the words it comes from, and you found those words in the file it names.
- Every row's check could fail: "the code is correct" is not a check; "the test for IT-0nn gives
  status needs-information" is.
- Each case of `docs/requirements.md` § Verification and each of the five queue rules has its own row.
- `git log --oneline -1` shows the spec commit.

Codex's summary of what it wrote is not the check. Open `planning/spec.md` and read it.
# Block 2. Plan: build steps with the test plan inside

A plan turns the spec into ordered steps before any code exists, so you can see and fix a wrong
order or a missing step while it costs nothing. The **test plan** sits inside the plan: one row per
case your tests must cover, each with the input, the mock response the test uses in place of the
model, and the **expected facts**. You write the expected facts from the message and the office
policy, never from the program's output: a test whose expected values were copied from the output
passes whatever the program does.

Start from your committed `planning/spec.md` (`docs/01-research-to-spec.md`).

## The planning skill

This repository supplies a skill for this block: `.agents/skills/plan-from-spec/SKILL.md`. A skill
is a folder of instructions Codex loads when a task matches it. This one tells Codex what the plan
holds and how to check it. Read it once before you start; it is one page.

## Steps

1. Start Codex in the root of your clone and ask it to use the plan-from-spec skill on
   `planning/spec.md`. Ask for the plan only, no code.

   <details><summary>An example request</summary>

   ```text
   Use the plan-from-spec skill on planning/spec.md. Write planning/plan.md only; write no code
   and no tests yet.
   ```

   </details>

2. Read `planning/plan.md` and correct it, with Codex or by hand, until each of these holds:
   - Every spec line appears in § Coverage with a step that builds it and a test or check that shows
     it. A spec line Codex left out goes back in.
   - The test plan has its own row for each case of `docs/requirements.md` § Verification: a
     complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure,
     an unchanged rerun, changed source content. Then the paraphrased request you author, a refusal
     or interrupted response, and a failed retry after a prior success.
   - Each row's input is a real export in `materials/requests/` (or the message you wrote), and you
     opened it and read the message.
   - Each expected fact quotes the message words and the policy rule it comes from. Work one row out
     yourself, from the message and the policy, before you accept Codex's version.
   - Each row's mock response is named: a saved reply under `tests/mock_responses/`, an error, or a
     cut-off reply. No test calls the real model, and none needs `API_KEY`.
   - The steps put the mock provider first, and each later step names the test written before it.
3. Commit the plan:

   ```bash
   git add planning/plan.md
   git commit -m "Plan: build steps and test plan"
   ```

## What is on disk at the end

`planning/plan.md`, committed, with four sections: Choices, Steps, Test plan, Coverage.

## How to tell it is right

- Count the spec's lines and the Coverage lines: the numbers match, or each missing line is under
  "Not yet covered" with its reason.
- Pick one test-plan row and check its expected facts against the message and the policy yourself.
  Every value has a quote beside it.
- `git log --oneline` shows the plan commit above the spec commit.
